case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: The holding is about the CFAA only. It leaves contract, trespass to chattels, copyright and state privacy claims fully available, and LinkedIn later prevailed on contract grounds.
case.holding: Scraping data that a website makes publicly available without any login does not amount to access without authorisation under the CFAA.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The principal authority that collecting public web data is not a federal computer crime, which is the first hurdle any web-scale training corpus has to clear.

reading.body:
The Ninth Circuit's 2022 ruling in hiQ v. LinkedIn established that scraping publicly available web data does not constitute unauthorized access under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, removing the primary federal criminal barrier for anyone building a large training corpus from the open web.

That holding matters for AI specifically because web-scale training data is the upstream input to the models that drive every downstream compute investment. A ruling the other way would have made assembling that data a federal offense, which no organization could accept regardless of how much infrastructure it was willing to build or buy. The CFAA question was, in that sense, a threshold one: it had to be cleared before any argument about cost, scale, or power capacity became relevant.

The data is precise about what the ruling does not cover. Contract claims, trespass to chattels, copyright, and state privacy law were all left intact, and LinkedIn subsequently prevailed against hiQ on contract grounds. The CFAA holding therefore narrows only one avenue of liability among several. Two live cases involving Perplexity AI appear in the data, signaling that web-scraping disputes remain active, but the data does not describe their claims or posture in enough detail to draw conclusions from them here.
